## A drone turns a list into a hierarchy

Put a low C underneath the notes of C major and the scale stops being seven
interchangeable pitches. Some of them settle into the drone. Others lean, and
they keep leaning even while you hold them perfectly still. One held bass note
supplies a centre, and the centre hands every other note a job.

Where a note sits relative to that centre is its *scale degree*. Degree 1, the
*tonic*, sounds like home. Degree 7 sits a semitone below it and presses upward,
which earns it the name leading tone. Degree 5, the dominant, holds a pause open
without closing it. None of that survives isolation. B on its own is a pitch; B
over a C drone is a sentence missing its last word.

## Eight notes over a held C

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 72
use_synth :tri

define :play_phrase do |notes|
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play pitch, release: 0.38, amp: 0.8
    sleep 0.5
  end
end

c_major = scale(:c4, :major).to_a

in_thread do
  play :c3, sustain: 15.5, release: 0.5, amp: 0.45
end

[[6, 7], [3, 2], [4, 4], [1, 0]].each do |from, to|
  play c_major[from], release: 0.7
  sleep 1
  play c_major[to], release: 0.9
  sleep 2
end

stem = [:c4, :e4, :g4, :a4, :g4, :e4]
[:f4, :g4, :b4, :c5].each do |ending|
  play_phrase stem + [ending, ending]
  sleep 1
end
```

`:tri` carries harmonics that meet the drone's, which is what lets a degree
either lock into the bass or grind against it; a sine has one partial and
nothing to lock with.

Take the two-note pairs first. B to C arrives hardest, because that semitone
closes right against the drone. F to E relaxes by the same small distance with
much less force behind it. G repeated rests without arriving. Then four longer
phrases share an identical opening and differ only in their last note. Rank
those four endings from most finished to least. Which one surprised you?

## Move the centre, keep the notes

1. Swap the drone to `:a2` and leave the melody exactly as it is. Same MIDI
   addresses, new centre. C turns into a colour inside A minor and stops being
   the convincing place to stop.
2. Change the B ending to `:bb4`. B-flat sits a whole tone under C, so the tight
   upward pull disappears. Compare them at the same tempo before you credit the
   accidental.
3. Raise the final G to `:g5`. Still degree 5, new register. Listen for whether
   the extra height exposes the ending, even though its function hasn't moved.

## Degree is an index, and the key is the scope

Scale degree is an index read against a tonic. Change the tonic and the same
MIDI number picks up a new index and a new tendency, exactly as an array offset
means nothing until you know which array is in scope.

No single mechanism produces all of this. Short distances invite motion, the
drone fixes how each note relates to the bass, and years of hearing tonal music
supply the rest. One held C won't separate those causes. It does give them a
stable reference to work against, which is why the four long phrases share an
opening and differ only in their final note.

## Rate your own tension

Build a hash mapping degrees 1 through 7 to your own tension rating from 0 to 5.
Start with `use_random_seed 42`, shuffle the degrees, and play each one over an
unchanged tonic drone. Leave two beats for your judgement, print the degree, and
then play the resolution route you chose.

Your ratings aren't answers to check against a key. What you're after is a
pattern you can hear twice.
